newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Peters says won't let paper upset relations.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Peters says won't let paper upset relations.

text.p: New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, labelled a loose cannon by an Australian government briefing paper, said on Sunday he would not let the document upset Wellington-Canberra relations.
Peters told TV1 television that the papers would be deeply embarrassing for Canberra "but we are not going to pay any attention to that or it will upset our relations with Australia".
A spokesman for Peters said the paper was merely the work of "an ignorant bureaucrat".
Peters told the Sunday Star Times newspaper such comments were normally just the opinion of a bureaucrat and often bore no resemblance to the opinion held by the minister.
"I personally have sought to discourage officials from making such extraordinary comments, which are clearly -- in this case -- well off the mark," he told the paper.

Peters, leader of the New Zealand First Party, is an extrovert politician who recently assaulted a government member of parliament in the house and late last year was involved in an early morning fracas with a journalist in a bar.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger and Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon declined to comment on the classified document which was obtained by Reuters after it was left on a table outside a Cairns hotel conference room where Pacific economic ministers were meeting.

The 93-page document was compiled by Australian foreign affairs staff to aid Foreign Minister Alexander Downer and as well as attacking Peters, slated a number of Pacific leaders as corrupt, incompetent or both.
The paper -- marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian eyes only -- warns New Zealand sometimes takes a contrary stand just to underline its own fading independence.

It said New Zealand -- the South Pacific's biggest power after Australia -- increasingly depended on Australia in defence and for trade, through the Closer Economic Relations (CER) free trade agreement.
But it added that Wellington sometimes frustrated Canberra's efforts to press economic reform on the region's shaky economies.
New Zealand opposition Foreign Affairs spokesman Mike Moore said the government was correct to not comment officially.
"It is embarrassing to everyone. It is particularly embarrassing to Australian officials who compiled the report and embarrassing to the New Zealand government," he told TV1.
South Pacific political analyst Anthony Haas said some of the comments about Pacific leaders in the Australian briefing were valid.

"I think it is a frank, fair and useful statement of unvarnished truth," he said. "I think they are home thoughts from abroad that should be taken seriously even though they sound pejorative and inevitably contemporary leaders will swing to their own defence."
Haas however was critical of the attack on Wellington's indulgent attitude to its Pacific neighbours in the paper.
"Australians who live in glass houses shouldn't be throwing stones," he said.
"The Australian record is far from perfect in the Pacific islands. Their policy formation process has gone through a number of convulsions over time," he said.
